title: Developer — Level 1: Foundations
description: Python fundamentals, basic data structures, HTTP, git, and SQL — the floor below which no interview proceeds.

questions.prompt: You need to check whether items exist in a collection millions of times. Why is a Python set/dict dramatically faster than a list?
options: Sets and dicts are hash tables with O(1) average lookup; a list must scan elements one by one, O(n)
Sets are stored on the GPU
Lists are always stored on disk
Sets keep elements sorted, enabling binary search
questions.answer_notes: `x in my_list` scans linearly; `x in my_set` hashes the element and jumps to a bucket — O(1) average. Millions of membership tests over thousands of items is the difference between milliseconds and minutes. Expect follow-ups: what makes an object hashable (stable __hash__ and __eq__, hence immutable keys), and worst-case O(n) on pathological collisions.
questions.difficulty_rationale: The single most common practical data-structure question.

questions.prompt: def add_item(item, items=[]): items.append(item); return items — what is wrong with this Python function?
options: The default list is created once at function definition and shared across calls, so items accumulate between unrelated calls
Nothing — this is idiomatic Python
Default arguments cannot be lists, so it raises a SyntaxError
append() returns None so the function always returns None
questions.answer_notes: Default values are evaluated once, at def time, not per call. Every call without the argument mutates the same list object — a classic source of ghostly bugs. Idiom: default to None and create the list inside (`if items is None: items = []`). This is a favorite screening question because it tests whether you understand Python's evaluation model rather than just syntax.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Canonical Python gotcha asked in most screens.

questions.prompt: In a REST API, what is the key property that GET, PUT, and DELETE share but POST does not?
options: Idempotency — repeating the request has the same effect as sending it once
They are encrypted while POST is not
They cannot carry a request body under any circumstances
They bypass authentication
questions.answer_notes: GET (safe and idempotent), PUT (replace — same result if repeated), DELETE (deleting twice = deleted) are idempotent; POST (create/append) is not — two POSTs make two resources. This matters for retries: proxies and clients may safely retry idempotent methods. Follow-ups: PATCH semantics, status codes (200/201/204/400/401/403/404/409/422/500), and why GET must never mutate state.
questions.difficulty_rationale: HTTP semantics floor for any web developer.

questions.prompt: Explain the difference between git merge and git rebase, and when you'd use each.
questions.answer_notes: Merge joins two branches with a merge commit, preserving both histories exactly as they happened — safe, non-destructive, the default for integrating into shared branches. Rebase replays your commits on top of the target branch, rewriting them (new hashes) into a linear history — cleaner to read and bisect, ideal for updating a private feature branch before review. Golden rule: never rebase commits that others may have based work on (shared/public history), because rewriting them forks reality. Bonus points: interactive rebase for cleaning a messy branch into logical commits before opening the PR, and knowing your team's convention (merge-commit vs squash vs rebase-merge) matters more than personal preference.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Asked constantly; also reveals collaboration habits.

questions.prompt: orders LEFT JOIN customers ON orders.customer_id = customers.id — what does the LEFT JOIN guarantee?
options: Every order appears in the result, with customer columns NULL where no matching customer exists
Every customer appears, with order columns NULL where they have no orders
Only rows where both sides match appear
The result is the cartesian product of both tables
questions.answer_notes: LEFT JOIN keeps all rows of the left table (orders), filling NULLs for missing right-side matches. INNER JOIN keeps only matches; RIGHT JOIN mirrors LEFT; FULL OUTER keeps both sides. Classic follow-up: find orders with no customer → LEFT JOIN … WHERE customers.id IS NULL. Also be ready to explain why a WHERE clause on the right table's columns silently turns a LEFT JOIN into an INNER JOIN (NULL rows fail the filter) — a beloved interview trap.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Bread-and-butter SQL every developer must answer instantly.

questions.prompt: What does professional error handling look like in a Python service? Cover what to catch, what never to do, and how errors should surface.
questions.answer_notes: Catch specific exceptions you can actually handle (retry a TimeoutError, return 404 on NotFound); let the rest propagate to a boundary handler that logs with full context (traceback, request ID) and maps to a clean API error. Never: bare `except:` or `except Exception: pass` (swallowing errors turns crashes into silent corruption), catching to just log-and-reraise at every layer (noise), or using exceptions for normal control flow. Practices: custom exception types per domain error, `raise ... from e` to preserve causal chains, context managers/finally for cleanup, and fail fast on programmer errors (let assertions and TypeErrors crash loudly in development). One log entry per failure, at the boundary, with context — not five copies at five layers.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Reveals production maturity more reliably than most algorithm questions.

questions.prompt: A function contains a loop over n items, and inside it performs a dict lookup and appends to a list. What is its time complexity?
options: O(n) — dict lookup and list append are O(1) average, executed n times
O(n²) — anything nested is quadratic
O(log n) — dictionaries use binary search
O(1) — modern computers parallelize loops automatically
questions.answer_notes: n iterations × O(1) work = O(n). The classic quadratic trap to contrast: using `item in some_list` inside the loop (O(n) each → O(n²)) or repeated string concatenation building an n-char string (O(n²) total; use join). Amortized O(1) for list append is worth mentioning by name. Interviewers often follow with: 'your endpoint got slow at 10k items — what do you look for?' Answer: accidental O(n²) via nested scans, N+1 queries.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Baseline complexity reasoning applied to everyday code.

questions.prompt: Why do Python projects use virtual environments and lock files?
options: To isolate each project's dependencies and pin exact versions, so builds are reproducible across machines and time
To make Python code run faster
To encrypt third-party packages
Because pip refuses to work without them
questions.answer_notes: Without isolation, projects fight over globally installed package versions; without pinning, `pip install` next month resolves different versions and 'works on my machine' becomes an incident. venv + a lock (pip-tools, poetry/uv lock, or pinned requirements.txt) gives reproducibility; requirements should separate direct from transitive deps. Same principle as package-lock.json in Node. Follow-up: how you upgrade safely — dedicated PR, CI, changelog review.
questions.difficulty_rationale: Basic professional hygiene; surprising how many candidates fumble it.
